New Mexico law sets out when a person occupying land can claim title by adverse possession, and how an owner can remove someone who has no right to be there.

What the official sources say

  • The statutory period for adverse possession in New Mexico is ten years. (NM Attorney General, Adverse Possession and Land Grants guide, citing NMSA 37-1-22; source)
  • Elements: open, continuous, exclusive, actual, visible, hostile and notorious possession for ten years; color of title; and payment of taxes. All must be met for the full 10 years. (NM AG guide; source)
  • The adverse possession statute requires the possessor to pay property taxes on the land; non-payment or interruption is fatal to the claim. (NM AG guide, citing NMSA 37-1-22; source)

New Mexico Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my New Mexico house?

Check the statute and talk to a New Mexico attorney about your facts.

Can someone become the owner of a New Mexico house just by living in it?

Only if they meet every element of the adverse possession statute for ten years, and that includes holding some written document that looks like a title and paying the property taxes. Section 37-1-22 NMSA 1978 is the controlling law. A person who occupies a vacant house without any paper claim, and without paying the tax bill, does not come close.

The statute asks for adverse possession "continuously and in good faith under color of title for ten years," with no lawsuit brought by the true owner in that time. When those conditions are met, the occupant may keep the land described in the writing that gives color of title, and an owner who sat on a claim for the ten years is barred. The statute defines adverse possession as "an actual and visible appropriation of land, commenced and continued under a color of title and claim of right inconsistent with and hostile to the claim of another."

The statute ends with a separate tax condition. Adverse possession is not established unless the party claiming it, or those the party claims through, continuously paid all state, county and municipal taxes assessed against the property during the ten years.

What are the elements a claimant has to prove?

The New Mexico Attorney General's guide on adverse possession, prepared by New Mexico Legal Aid for the Land Grant Council, sums them up as three groups. The claimant needs open, continuous, exclusive, actual, visible, hostile and notorious possession for ten years, color of title, and payment of taxes. The guide says all of them must be met for the full ten years, and that failing any one defeats the claim.

  • Continuous: possession cannot be intermittent.
  • Actual: the claimant must physically enter. The guide says holding a deed is not enough, because the ten years do not begin until the claimant enters and takes possession.
  • Open and notorious: the claimant cannot hide. The clock does not run until the possession is visible enough to give the owner notice.
  • Exclusive: possession cannot be shared with the public or other users. If others try to use the land, the claimant has to keep them out.
  • Hostile: the occupant must be there without any right or permission, so that the possession is plainly against the owner's rights.

The annotations add that the claimant carries the burden. A party must prove adverse possession by clear and convincing evidence, and it cannot be established by inference or implication.

What is color of title, and what counts?

Color of title is a written document that purports to give the occupant title, even if it turns out to be defective. The Attorney General guide lists documents New Mexico courts have accepted: quitclaim deeds, a certificate of sale for taxes, a government patent, a void deed, and a quiet title decree or other court judgment.

The annotations to 37-1-22 give more detail. A recorded quitclaim deed, executed and acknowledged one day and recorded the next, with the buyer taking immediate possession, established color of title in one case. A tax deed can serve even when void for lack of title in the grantor, but not if its land description is too weak to identify the property. In one case involving siblings who owned together, a deed to one sibling and his wife did not establish color of title.

For owners, the lesson is that a stray deed in the record can matter. If someone is living in your house and has recorded a deed, even a weak one, the ten-year clock may have started. Our New Mexico quitclaim deed guide explains the form that often shows up in these disputes.

Does a tenant or a guest ever become an adverse possessor?

Almost never, because permission defeats hostility. The annotations say that where the original entry was permissive, the statute of limitations does not begin to run until an adverse holding is declared and notice of the change reaches the owner. Mere possession is not enough. Possession that starts as a tenancy is presumed permissive, and ending that presumption takes proof or a presumption of notice to the owner that the occupant now claims against them.

A person who enters a vacant house without permission is in a different position, but the extra requirements still apply. The Attorney General guide describes cases where claimants won by marking boundaries, posting no-trespassing signs, clearing land, fencing, limiting access and paying taxes. Those facts, taken together, gave the owner notice. Simply staying in a house, with none of those steps, is thin evidence.

The statute also protects some owners with a disability. If the person entitled to sue was imprisoned, of unsound mind or under the age of majority when the cause of action first accrued, they get one year after the disability ends to bring suit. The statute says cumulative disabilities do not extend the bar.

What about government land, water rights and land grants?

The statute does not reach every kind of property. The Attorney General guide says adverse possession usually cannot be applied against governmental property, only private property. It also explains that land grants governed as political subdivisions were made immune from adverse possession claims in 2007 under 49-1-11.2, except for claims that had already vested by June 15, 2007.

The annotations add two more limits. New Mexico's water code means water rights cannot be obtained through adverse possession, and the state's rights in highways cannot be divested by it under a cross-referenced statute.

How does an owner remove someone who has no right to be there?

Through a court case. The New Mexico Courts self-help guide says a landlord must go to court before evicting a tenant, and that a person living in a home who is not on the lease cannot be evicted like a tenant. That person is removed through "forcible entry," using Form 4-203, Complaint in Forcible Entry. At the hearing, the judge decides whether the person must leave and how much time they have to move out.

Section 35-10-1 NMSA 1978 lists the grounds for a forcible entry or unlawful detainer action in magistrate court. The first applies directly to uninvited occupants: the defendant entered and occupied the land of another against the owner's will or consent and refused to vacate after notice from the owner, agent or attorney. The other grounds cover:

  • A tenant who holds over after the lease ends or contrary to its terms.
  • A tenant who fails to pay rent when due.
  • An occupant who stays after a mortgage foreclosure or execution sale, unless claiming title paramount to the mortgage or derived from the purchaser.
  • A month-to-month tenant or tenant at will who stays after thirty days' written notice to vacate.

The district court has concurrent jurisdiction when the rent or reasonable rental value is $50 or more per month. An annotation also notes that these actions are summary proceedings that settle nothing about title. A forcible entry case puts the parties back in their prior positions but does not decide who owns the house.

When is trespassing a crime in New Mexico?

Section 30-14-1.1 NMSA 1978 makes several kinds of trespass a misdemeanor. A person who enters and remains on the lands of another after having been requested to leave commits one. So does a person who enters land posted against trespass at every roadway or apparent way of access, and a person who drives a vehicle onto fenced land except through an apparent way of access.

The same section creates civil liability. A person who enters another's land without permission and damages the realty or its improvements, including buildings, structures, trees and shrubs, owes double the appraised value of the damage to the owner, lessee or person in lawful possession.

The offense turns on a request to leave, so a dated written request is worth keeping. Talk to an attorney before acting.

What should an owner do to protect a vacant or inherited house?

Keep the paper record clean and the taxes current. Several steps follow from the statute and the guides:

  • Visit the property on a schedule, and document each visit with dates and photos.
  • Post no-trespassing signs and keep the property secured.
  • Pay the property tax yourself. The tax condition in the statute means a claimant who has not paid cannot succeed, and a delinquency can lead to a tax sale, covered in our New Mexico tax deed guide.
  • Check the county clerk's records for any deed or affidavit recorded by someone else.
  • Give written notice to anyone staying without permission, and keep a copy.

An annotation to the Property Tax Code, citing a 1954 decision, says the general rule is that continuity of adverse possession is interrupted if the land is forfeited to the state for taxes. That is one more reason to keep the tax record current.

Owners who inherited a house and cannot manage an occupant, repairs or back taxes sometimes sell as-is. Cash Home Buyers does not promise a price in advance. Anyone who buys will want to know who lives in the house and whether a court case is pending, so share that up front.

More questions about New Mexico Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession

How long does adverse possession take in New Mexico?

Ten years of continuous possession under color of title, in good faith, with all taxes paid, under 37-1-22 NMSA 1978. The claimant must prove it by clear and convincing evidence.

Do squatters have rights in New Mexico?

A person without a written claim to title and without paying the property taxes cannot meet the statute. The owner removes an occupant through a forcible entry complaint in court.

Do adverse possession claimants have to pay property taxes?

Yes. The statute says adverse possession is not established unless the claimant or predecessors continuously paid all state, county and municipal taxes assessed during the ten years.

How do I remove someone who is not on the lease?

The New Mexico Courts self-help guide says to file Form 4-203, Complaint in Forcible Entry. The judge decides whether the person must leave and sets the time to move out.

Is it a crime to stay on someone's land after being told to leave?

Yes. Section 30-14-1.1 makes it a misdemeanor to enter and remain on the lands of another after having been requested to leave.

Can someone claim a New Mexico house after an eviction-type dispute?

A forcible entry or unlawful detainer case does not decide title, according to the annotations to 35-10-1. A separate action would be needed to settle ownership.

New Mexico Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

New Mexico statutes set the basic rules between landlords and tenants, including deposits, notices and what happens when a rental is sold.

What the official sources say

  • For rental agreements under one year, the owner shall not demand or receive a deposit above one month's rent; for annual agreements a deposit above one month's rent requires the owner to pay annual interest to the resident. (NMSA 47-8-18(A); source)
  • The owner must give an itemized written list of deductions and the balance within thirty days of termination of the rental agreement or resident departure, whichever is later; no deposit may be retained for normal wear and tear. (NMSA 47-8-18(C); source)
Selling in New Mexico?
We buy New Mexico houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Which law covers landlords and tenants in New Mexico?

The Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act, found in Chapter 47, Article 8 of the New Mexico Statutes, sets the main rules for residential rentals. The act calls landlords "owners" and tenants "residents," so searches for "New Mexico tenant rights" lead back to that wording.

The rules cover deposits, entry, rent, late fees, notices and retaliation. They matter to a seller because a rented house is sold subject to what the act requires of the owner, and a buyer or showing schedule has to fit around the resident's rights.

The table below gathers the rules most often needed in a sale. Each figure comes from the statute text for the section named.

TopicRuleSection
Deposit, lease under one yearNo more than one month's rent47-8-18(A)(2)
Deposit refund or itemized listWithin thirty days of termination or departure, whichever is later47-8-18(C)
Bad faith deposit retention$250 civil penalty payable to the resident47-8-18(E)
Entry to inspect or show the unitTwenty-four hours written notice unless agreed otherwise47-8-24(A)
Late feeUp to five percent of rent per period, if the agreement provides for it47-8-15(D)
Rent increaseWritten notice at least thirty days before the rental date or the end of the term47-8-15(F)
Month-to-month terminationWritten notice at least thirty days before the rental date47-8-37(B)
Nonpayment of rentThree days after written notice47-8-33(D)

How do security deposits work?

A New Mexico owner may take a reasonable deposit to cover damage during the residency, and for rental agreements shorter than one year the deposit cannot exceed one month's rent. Under an annual agreement, a deposit above one month's rent requires the owner to pay the resident interest each year.

The owner may apply the deposit to unpaid rent and to damage caused by the resident's noncompliance, but no deposit may be kept for normal wear and tear. The owner then has thirty days to mail an itemized written list of deductions and any balance to the resident's last known address.

Missing that deadline is costly. The statute says the owner forfeits the right to withhold any part of the deposit, to counterclaim in a suit over it and to bring a separate action for damage to the property. The owner is also liable for court costs and reasonable attorney fees. A 2025 Court of Appeals decision noted in the annotations confirmed that the forfeiture applies when the owner fails to itemize, and that a timely itemization keeps a later damage claim alive.

For a seller, the practical point is the thirty-day clock. If a tenant moves out around closing, the clock runs from the later of termination or departure, and the sale contract should say who handles the itemization.

Can a landlord enter to show the house to buyers?

Yes, with notice. Section 47-8-24 lets an owner enter a dwelling to exhibit it to prospective or actual purchasers, along with inspections, repairs and showings to mortgagees or contractors.

Unless the owner and resident agree otherwise, the owner must first give twenty-four hours written notice stating the intent to enter, the purpose, the date and a reasonable estimate of the time frame. Entry without consent is allowed in an emergency, and the notice rule does not apply to repairs within seven days of a resident's request or to entry with a public official or a utility representative.

  • If the resident offers reasonable alternate dates, the owner must try to accommodate them when practicable and not economically harmful.
  • The owner may not abuse the right of access.
  • If the resident refuses lawful access, the owner can seek an injunction to compel access or terminate the agreement, and can recover damages.
  • If the owner enters unlawfully or makes repeated demands that interfere with quiet enjoyment, the resident can seek an injunction or terminate the agreement and recover damages.

This is why a rented house is slower to show than a vacant one. Every open house or buyer walkthrough needs written notice.

What are the rules on rent, late fees and increases?

Rent is due at the time agreed, and a late fee is allowed only if the rental agreement provides for one. A 2025 amendment effective June 20, 2025 cut the cap on late fees from ten percent to five percent of rent per rental period.

Late fees can be calculated only on rent. Deposits, additional fees and utilities are excluded from the calculation. To charge the fee, the owner must give notice of it no later than the last day of the next rental period after the default. An older Court of Appeals case denied late fees to landlords who did not give that notice.

An owner may raise rent in a month-to-month residency by written notice at least thirty days before the periodic rental date. For a fixed term, the notice must come at least thirty days before the term ends. Unless both sides agree in writing, rent paid cannot be allocated to deposits or damages.

How can an owner end a tenancy or evict for nonpayment?

Notices in New Mexico are short and must follow the statute exactly. For nonpayment, the resident has three days after written notice of nonpayment and the owner's intent to terminate. Paying the full amount in the manner stated in the notice before the three days expire bars an action for nonpayment.

A 2023 Court of Appeals decision held that an owner cannot file a petition for restitution until the day after the third day has passed. Filing on day three was premature and the petition should have been dismissed.

For other breaches, Section 47-8-33 sets a different path.

  • A first material breach requires a written notice describing the dates and facts, saying the agreement ends in not less than seven days if the breach is not remedied.
  • A second material breach within six months allows a notice that terminates the agreement not less than seven days after receipt.
  • The notice must be given within thirty days of the breach or knowledge of it.
  • A substantial violation allows a three-day termination notice, with defenses for domestic violence victims and for residents who could not have known of or prevented the violation.
  • If a deadline to remedy falls on a weekend or federal holiday, it extends to the next business day.

Relief in court can be based only on the grounds stated in the written notice. For month-to-month tenancies, either side may end the residency by thirty days written notice before the rental date. Week-to-week residencies need seven days. If a resident holds over without consent, the owner may sue for possession, and for damages and attorney fees if the holdover is willful and not in good faith.

What counts as retaliation?

An owner cannot raise rent, cut services or bring or threaten an action for possession because the resident did something protected within the previous six months. The protected acts listed in Section 47-8-39 include complaining to a code enforcement agency about a health and safety violation, joining a residents' association, making a written repair request, filing a fair housing complaint, testifying for another resident and abating rent as the act allows.

The protection applies to a resident who is in compliance with the rental agreement. If the owner retaliates, the resident gets the remedies in Section 47-8-48 and can raise the violation as a defense to an eviction.

There is an exception. An owner may raise rent or change services at the end of a term if the change matches what other residents of similar units receive and is not aimed at one resident. A seller who plans to list a rented home should avoid timing a notice right after a repair complaint.

What should an owner know before selling a rented house?

The statutes cited here do not say that a sale ends a lease, so an owner should assume the rental agreement and the act continue to apply until a lawyer confirms otherwise. What the act does cover is how you show the house, how you treat the deposit and when you can end the tenancy.

  • Give written twenty-four hour notice for each showing, inspection or appraisal visit.
  • Keep records of rent paid, late fee notices and any repair requests.
  • Do not serve a termination or rent increase notice in a way that looks aimed at a resident who complained.
  • Decide in writing who is responsible for the deposit and the thirty-day itemization if the resident leaves around closing.
  • Check the agreement for deposit terms, because a deposit above one month's rent on an annual lease carries yearly interest.

Selling to a cash buyer can simplify some of this. Cash Home Buyers purchases houses with tenants in place and as they are, so you do not need to finish repairs or empty the unit first. Terms vary by property, and a lawyer should review the lease before you sign anything.

More questions about New Mexico Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

How much can a New Mexico landlord charge for a security deposit?

For a rental agreement shorter than one year, no more than one month's rent. Under an annual agreement a larger deposit is allowed, but the owner must then pay the resident annual interest on it. The rule is in NMSA 47-8-18(A).

How long does a landlord have to return a deposit in New Mexico?

Thirty days from the end of the rental agreement or the resident's departure, whichever is later. If deductions are taken, the owner must send an itemized written list with the balance. Failing to do so forfeits the right to withhold and exposes the owner to court costs and attorney fees.

How much notice must a landlord give to enter a rental?

Twenty-four hours in writing, unless the owner and resident agree otherwise. The notice must state the purpose and the date and a reasonable time frame. Emergencies and repairs requested by the resident within seven days are exceptions.

What is the maximum late fee in New Mexico?

Five percent of the rent for each rental period in default, and only if the rental agreement provides for a late fee. The cap was lowered from ten percent effective June 20, 2025. The owner must give notice of the fee by the end of the next rental period.

How long is the notice to leave for nonpayment of rent?

Three days after written notice of nonpayment and the owner's intent to terminate. If the resident pays everything due in the manner the notice states before the three days end, the owner cannot proceed on that nonpayment.

New Mexico Tax Deed and Tax Lien Sales: Process, Redemption and Selling First

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

When property tax goes unpaid in New Mexico, the statutes allow the taxing authority to sell a lien or the property itself, and they give the owner a set time to redeem.

What the official sources say

  • New Mexico's Taxation and Revenue Department Property Tax Division sells delinquent real property at public auction (NMSA 7-38-65), usually at the county courthouse. (NM TRD, Delinquent Property Tax Auctions; source)
  • A sale properly made under 7-38-67 constitutes full payment of delinquent taxes, penalties and interest; the sale extinguishes only the tax lien, not other liens. (NM TRD, Delinquent Property Tax Auctions; source)
  • The former owner has a two-year period to challenge the sale in court under 7-38-70; the only redemption period is the 120-day federal IRS redemption period. (NM TRD, Delinquent Property Tax Auctions; source)
Selling in New Mexico?
We buy New Mexico houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

When does unpaid property tax lead to a sale in New Mexico?

The state can sell a house at public auction once its taxes have been delinquent for three years. Section 7-38-65 NMSA 1978 says real property may be sold for delinquent taxes at any time after three years from the first date shown on the tax delinquency list on which the taxes became delinquent. The sale must be offered within four years of that date, with an extension if a court or other legal bar prevents it.

The debt starts earlier than the sale. Under 7-38-48, taxes on real property are a lien against the property from January 1 of the tax year, and the lien is a first lien that outranks every other interest, perfected or not. The lien continues until the taxes, penalty and interest are paid.

Interest runs on its own clock. Section 7-38-49 says that if taxes are not paid within thirty days after they are due, interest accrues from the thirtieth day at one percent a month or any fraction of a month. Interest is not charged on interest or on any penalty.

A 2013 amendment, effective January 1, 2014, requires the department to offer at least one property from each county's delinquency list for sale every year, unless the department director and the county treasurer agree in writing to postpone.

Does New Mexico sell tax liens or the property itself?

The sources reviewed for this page describe a sale of the real property itself, followed by a deed. The Taxation and Revenue Department's Property Tax Division sells delinquent real property at public auction under 7-38-65, usually at the county courthouse or a similar location the department designates in the county where the property sits. The sources do not describe a sale of tax lien certificates to investors.

County treasurers have a separate tool for mobile homes. The department's auction page explains that under 7-38-53 the county treasurer may seize a mobile home and sell it for taxes under a demand warrant.

The department does not hold sales in all 33 counties every year. Its page says there is no fixed schedule, and sales are scheduled as title research is completed and other collection efforts are exhausted. When the page was last updated, it listed a San Miguel County auction on November 19, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. Check the current list at the department's auction page or call the Property Tax Division at (505) 827-0883.

How does the auction work, step by step?

The auction follows requirements in 7-38-67 and the department's published terms. The main points:

  • Notice: published in a local newspaper at least once a week for the three weeks before the week of the sale, stating the time, place and a property description.
  • Location: held in the county where the property is located, by the department or a hired auctioneer.
  • Minimum price: not less than the total of delinquent taxes, penalties, interest and costs. The department must also consider the value of the owner's interest when setting it.
  • Registration: bidders register on the day of sale. The department's FAQ says registration begins at 8 a.m. and closes at 10 a.m. when the auction starts.
  • Bidding: oral, in person or through an agent with a notarized authorization.
  • Payment: in full by the close of the auction, by cashier's check, money order, or a personal or company check backed by a bank letter of guarantee.

If a property does not sell, it may be offered later, but the notice requirements apply again to each sale. The department may re-offer a property for less than the minimum bid if it did not sell for at least that amount.

How can an owner stop the sale?

By paying everything owed, or signing an installment agreement, by 5:00 p.m. on the day before the sale. Section 7-38-65 lists both options: all delinquent taxes, penalties, interest and costs paid by that deadline, or a written installment agreement under 7-38-68 entered by then.

The installment agreement has limits worth knowing:

  • It cannot run more than thirty-six months.
  • Interest accrues on the unpaid balance at one percent a month.
  • Signing it is an irrevocable admission of liability for the taxes covered.
  • As long as the terms are met, it prevents further collection action on those taxes.
  • The division may proceed with collection if payments are missed, other property taxes go unpaid, or another condition is broken.
  • After a breach, the original delinquency date is used for timing a sale, and the division will not enter another agreement for the same taxes.
  • The division cannot enter an agreement on or after the date of the initial sale.

What rights does a former owner have after the sale?

New Mexico does not give former owners a right of redemption, but they have two years to challenge the sale in court. The department's FAQ states that the state has no right of redemption for former owners. It describes the two-year period under 7-38-70 as the window in which the former owner, or someone claiming through them, can bring a court challenge. The only redemption period the department mentions is the 120-day federal IRS redemption period, which applies if the federal government holds a lien on the property.

Section 7-38-70 sets out what a challenger must prove to defeat the buyer's title. Any one of the following is enough:

  • The property was not subject to taxation for the tax years in question.
  • The division failed to mail the required notice or to receive any required return receipt.
  • The challenger had title at the time of sale and had paid all delinquent amounts before it.
  • The challenger had an installment agreement and made every payment on time.

Annotations show that courts also look at notice. One case found notice constitutionally inadequate when it went only to an old address after the owner had filed a change of address with the assessor. A 2024 Court of Appeals decision, Dearborn v. Clarke, held that the department can invalidate a tax sale that was not conducted in substantial compliance with the tax code, so long as no deed has been issued. In that case the sole bidder paid the minimum price of $17,100.

What does the buyer receive, and what stays on the property?

The buyer receives a tax deed that works like a quitclaim and carries no warranty. The department says the deed conveys all of the former owner's interest as of the date the state's lien arose, subject only to perfected interests existing before that date. It adds that the sale extinguishes the tax lien only. No other liens are extinguished, and the buyer must inspect the property and review the chain of title before bidding.

QuestionWhat the department or statute saysSource
Which liens does the sale remove?The tax lien only; other liens are not extinguishedTRD auction FAQ, 7-38-67
What kind of deed?A tax deed, treated as equivalent to a quitclaim; no title warrantyTRD auction FAQ
When can the buyer enter?Not until the division delivers the deedTRD auction terms
Refund if rescinded?Only the amount paid at the sale, with no interest or buyer expensesTRD auction terms
Does the sale price set the new tax value?No; the county assessor determines valueTRD auction FAQ

Sales are as-is, final and without refunds, and the buyer indemnifies the department for environmental conditions, according to the department's terms. Buyers cannot trespass while inspecting.

Is it better to sell before the auction?

For an owner with equity, selling first is often worth checking, because the minimum bid is set by the debt rather than by the home's value. Section 7-38-67 sets the minimum price at the taxes, penalties, interest and costs owed. A bidder can win at that number if nobody offers more. An annotation to 7-38-67 describes the department's duty to recognize the owner's interest in any amount above the debt, but the owner is not in control of how high bidding goes.

A private sale that closes before the deadline gives the owner control of the price and the timing. The title company can pay the delinquent taxes, penalties, interest and costs from the proceeds at closing, which satisfies the condition in 7-38-65 if it is done by 5:00 p.m. the day before the auction. The sale needs a buyer who can close quickly and accept the house in its present condition.

Cash Home Buyers buys New Mexico houses as-is and does not promise a price in advance. If your home is on a delinquency list or you have received a sale notice, tell any buyer the auction date at the start, because the closing has to be scheduled around it. A tax attorney or the Property Tax Division can confirm the payoff figure.

More questions about New Mexico Tax Deed and Tax Lien Sales

How long before New Mexico can sell my house for back taxes?

At least three years after the first date the taxes appear on the delinquency list. Under 7-38-65 the property must then be offered within four years of that date, unless a legal bar delays it.

Does New Mexico have a redemption period after a tax sale?

No, the Taxation and Revenue Department says the state has no right of redemption for former owners. The only redemption period it mentions is the 120-day federal IRS period. Former owners have two years to challenge the sale in court under 7-38-70.

Does a tax sale wipe out my mortgage?

The department says the sale extinguishes the tax lien only and no other liens. The deed is subject to perfected interests that existed before the property tax lien arose. Ask an attorney how that applies to your loan.

Can I make payments instead of losing the house?

Yes, through an installment agreement under 7-38-68, if signed by 5:00 p.m. the day before the sale. It runs up to thirty-six months at one percent monthly interest, and the division cannot enter one on or after the initial sale date.

How much interest accrues on unpaid New Mexico property tax?

One percent a month or any fraction of a month, starting on the thirtieth day after the tax is due, under 7-38-49. No interest is charged on interest or on any penalty.

Where are New Mexico tax auctions held?

Usually at the county courthouse or a similar location the department designates in the county where the property sits. The department does not hold sales in all 33 counties each year.
